ctx.x: No. Here’s what happened. Erroll had actually gone over to Mercury Records for a while. I can’t remember now what the dispute was. I hate to say it, but I think Martha had had a fight with Mitch, because Mitch didn’t want to put out singles by Erroll, because they didn’t sell. She wanted them out, because no other pianist had them out. You know Martha. She thought there would be more airplay. She was probably right, but it wasn’t in Columbia’s interests to do that for no great reason, because we were doing so…

We’re free.” “Good,” I said. “Welcome home.” She sent it to me and called me a couple of days later and said, “How do you like it?” I said, “You’re right. It’s magnificent, but the recording is terrible. I hope I can fix it up.” I said, “We’ll do it, because I don’t think he’ll ever play that great for a whole night again.” I’m sure he did, but it never got caught on records. I sweated with that…

ctx.x: Well it’s a pretty astute balance of artistic and commercial concerns.

Well that’s true you had to do that in order to stand out. Now I don’t like to talk against competition but take Norman Granz’s operation which was eventually the Verve label and all. Norman made a tremendous number of records but his approach was basically to just bring the guys into the studio or record them on stage, and then figure out what to do about packaging and there was never any really concept in any of the albums. I’m sorry to single out Norman, but it’s an easy target for this idea of you can go two…
albums that have an identity and significance within simply themselves, instead of just being part of the body of work of an artist.
